<reason>Both sides argued well, and the debate narrowed cleanly to two decision rules. PRO's strongest work was rhetorical and conceptual: the bedside script reframe, the "opt-in also guesses, and guesses wrong more often" symmetry, and the devastating catch that CON's alleged harm is defined so it can never appear in any refusal rate, complaint, or repeal. That pressure was real, and PRO handled its own pressure questions honestly. But PRO carries the burden on the first prong ("measurably increase"), and it is precisely there that PRO's case eroded: it conceded that the default cannot be isolated from the reform package, conceded Wales produced no clean jump, and then still leaned on cross-country clustering — an inconsistency CON caught precisely ([B4.6]). CON also answered PRO's central dilemma with a clean, non-evasive distinction (a rule can be unjust without being effective) and preserved the act/omission asymmetry ("withholding a taking is not authorizing one"), which blunted PRO's guess-symmetry move. CON's closing stated the sharpest decision rule available: the motion is about the shift, and if coordinators do the lifting, the shift does not — a burden PRO reframed rather than discharged. CON's own concession that harm "need not show up" in refusal data cost it the family-distress prong, but the asymmetric burden structure (PRO must win all three prongs; CON needs only one) means that cost is smaller. Add PRO's clipped rebuttal as an execution cost, and CON edges a competitive debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's answer to PRO's "pick one" dilemma — that soft presumed consent can mislabel and wrong people while still not delivering the surge, because organs only move through referral, timing and family acquiescence — because it both dissolved PRO's central trap and set up the closing decision rule that PRO had conceded the default cannot be isolated from coordinators.</best_rebuttal>
